items.title: JetBrains Air Ships Natively in 2026.3 IDEs as a Multi-Agent Orchestration Layer
items.summary: From the 2026.3 release wave (early November), JetBrains Air is built into all JetBrains IDEs rather than sold as a closed assistant. It connects first-party and third-party agents — Claude Agent, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Junie out of the box, plus Gemini CLI, OpenCode and Antigravity via the ACP registry — and lets developers run them in parallel Git worktrees with IDE-level diff review, refactors and debugger access. Local sessions use your own ChatGPT/Copilot/Google/Claude subscriptions or API keys (no JetBrains AI plan required), and Junie Lite is free with a JetBrains account.
items.impact: This is the clearest signal yet that the IDE is becoming a neutral command center for competing coding agents instead of a single-vendor chatbot. The 'bring-your-own-agent' model shifts leverage to the developer and makes multi-agent coordination, not model access, the real product surface.

items.title: Google Winds Down Jules, Consolidating Its Async Coding Agent Into Antigravity
items.summary: Announced October 29 and effective now: Jules stopped accepting new sessions on November 11 and turned read-only through December 31, when it shuts down entirely. Google frames the move as unifying its agentic-coding efforts; learnings flow into the agent-first platform Antigravity, which gained a plugin marketplace (Atlassian, Figma, Stripe, Datadog and others) the same day. Code, branches and PRs already live in GitHub and are unaffected, but settings, memories, scheduled tasks and session history must be exported via the Jules Tools CLI before year-end.
items.impact: The closure of a flagship async coding agent shows the market is consolidating around a few integrated platforms rather than many standalone agents. Teams relying on cloud background tasks should migrate now and treat agent data export as a routine offboarding step.

items.title: Gartner Publishes Its First Magic Quadrant for AI Agent Management Platforms
items.summary: Gartner's inaugural Magic Quadrant for AI Agent Management Platforms (report dated October 27) names Microsoft, IBM and ServiceNow as Leaders, with AWS, Salesforce, OneReach.ai and Gravitee as Challengers. The category covers agent discovery, lifecycle management, guardrails, evaluation, identity/access, integration controls and cost tracking — and Gartner forecasts that by 2029, 60% of AI agents will be managed through such a platform and over 35% of enterprise AI run-budgets will be routed on verified business outcomes.
items.impact: Agent governance and 'tokenomics' just became their own software category with an analyst scorecard. For anyone running more than a handful of agents, the signal is clear: discovery, ownership and per-task cost tracking are becoming table stakes, not nice-to-haves.

items.title: Tsinghua, Wubu XinQiong and AgiBot Demo Collective Experience Learning Across 96 Humanoids
items.summary: A joint industry-academia team introduced Collective Experience Learning (CEL), a paradigm where robots share successes and failures instead of each being hand-taught. Validated on 96 real humanoids performing five home and industrial tasks (flower arranging, folding, phone charging, stool assembly, phone packaging), the group reached a 97.5% overall success rate — beating the average of six human operators — with the hardest task rising from 79.2% to 98.3%. A fault-tolerant async training system (FATS) kept hardware-failure overhead to just 1.3% of runtime, and scaling from 16 to 96 robots further improved capability.
items.impact: CEL attacks the core scaling bottleneck of embodied AI: human demonstration can't keep pace with fleet size. Turning experience-sharing into a system primitive could make large-scale robot deployment a point of continuous improvement rather than a one-time training cost.

items.title: Agility Robotics Lists on Nasdaq as AGLT, First U.S. Pure-Play Humanoid Company to Go Public
items.summary: On November 5, Agility Robotics began trading on Nasdaq under ticker AGLT after merging with Churchill Capital Corp XI, raising roughly $465M in gross capital. The company enters public markets with more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation and over $300M in committed multi-year orders for its next-generation Digit 5 humanoid, with deployments at GXO, Schaeffler and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada and a U.S. RoboFab capacity of up to 10,000 robots per year.
items.impact: A pure-play humanoid company reaching public markets is a milestone for embodied intelligence as an investable asset class. It sets a financial benchmark — and a scrutiny bar — for the whole sector as vendors shift from demos to commercial fleets.
